decisions.quote: Depression risk genes in combination with childhood events have been associated with biased processing as an intermediate phenotype for depression. The aim of the present conceptual replication study was to investigate the role of biased automatic approach-avoidance tendencies as a candidate intermediate phenotype for depression, in the context of genes (5-HTTLPR polymorphism) and childhood trauma. A naturalistic remitted depressed patients sample (N = 209) performed an Approach-Avoidance Task (AAT) with facial expressions (angry, sad, happy and neutral).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree that the record is a completed empirical replication ('conceptual replication study') analyzing AAT, 5-HTTLPR genotype, and childhood trauma data in 209 remitted depressed patients to test whether earlier G x E intermediate-phenotype findings hold for automatic approach-avoidance tendencies.

decisions.quote: In line with Seidel and colleagues [ 42 ], we expected automatic avoidance of angry faces as well. We did not find this, however. The present results are tentative, but perhaps the signaling of sad rather than angry expressions is most relevant for depression. This would correspond with information processing models in depression: Sad faces are congruent to depressed patients’ mood state, activating depressotypic schemas, which lead to biased processing. This is corroborated by our finding that symptoms of social anxiety (LSAS) did not influence results.

Current remitted population, absence of matched never-depressed controls and new sad-face/genetic/trauma results remain explicit; changed method/population alone do not erase an author-stated comparison. Generic support for GxEtheory does not override the named original nonfinding. No exact Seidel design/statistical replication is claimed.

decisions.quote: Although we do not have previous genetic research to base our hypotheses on, based on clinical experiences, information processing theories in depression and the research by Seidel and colleagues [ 42 ], we expected avoidance of negative (sad, angry) facial expressions in remitted depressed S/L g -carriers who have experienced childhood trauma, as this represents the most vulnerable subgroup. Following Culverhouse and colleagues [ 9 ], we expected a main effect of childhood trauma on automatic approach-avoidance tendencies in depression. Materials and methods Participants This study is part of the ‘Info in Genes’ study, which involves a total of 337 remitted depressed patients. In the ‘Info in Genes’ study, the role of cognitive biases and genetic susceptibility to depression is investigated by assessing biased processing in several domains in remitted depressed patients [ 20 , 21 , 22 ].
decisions.reason: Shipped row 937 (the sole shipped row for this paper) lists Vrijsen et al. (2014) [20] as the target original, and the initial expert retained it based on the broad Discussion sentence stating that the study 'partly supports earlier G x E findings... [ 10 , 11 , 14 , 16 – 22 ]'. However, the full text establishes that: (1) this study is part of the same 'Info in Genes' cohort of 337 remitted depressed patients as Vrijsen et al. [20, 21, 22], which assessed other cognitive-bias domains in that cohort and provided the childhood-trauma coding; (2) the citation range [10, 11, 14, 16–22] mixes theoretical reviews ([11, 14]), community attention studies, and same-programme papers without retesting any specific published empirical finding of Vrijsen et al. (2014); and (3) the authors explicitly state that their 5-HTTLPR x childhood trauma objective on the Approach-Avoidance Task (AAT) is tested for the first time here ('To our knowledge, the current study is the first study with this objective'; 'we do not have previous genetic research to base our hypotheses on'). The actual published empirical AAT finding in depression that the authors explicitly base their directional prediction on and test against their data is Seidel et al. (2010) [42] (automatic avoidance of angry faces in depression), matching blind target 0 and resolving the dependent target binding on row 937.
